explanation: Off-by-one: changing <= to < means the last upvalue index is excluded from the valid range, causing getupvalref to return &nullup for the last valid upvalue, but lua_upvaluejoin then dereferences it expecting a valid UpVal pointer, leading to null/invalid dereference.

Off-by-one in upvalue copy loop in lua_pushcclosure: loop runs n+1 times, reading one stack slot beyond the n upvalues, writing it into cl->upvalue[n] which is beyond the allocated closure upvalue array.

diff.before: api_check(L, idx <= MAXUPVAL + 1, "upvalue index too large");

explanation: Off-by-one in upvalue index check in index2value: MAXUPVAL is 255, so MAXUPVAL+1=256 should be the max valid idx, but changing <= to < rejects idx==256 (MAXUPVAL+1) while allowing idx==255 to pass through and potentially access one slot beyond the upvalue array.

explanation: Off-by-one in lua_checkstack: changing > to >= means we skip growing the stack when exactly n slots are available (stack_last - top == n), but then ci->top is set to top+n which equals stack_last, allowing subsequent pushes to go one past the stack boundary.

diff.before: api_check(L, n <= MAXUPVAL, "upvalue index too large");
diff.after: api_check(L, n < MAXUPVAL, "upvalue index too large");

explanation: Off-by-one in lua_pushcclosure upvalue count check: MAXUPVAL=255 upvalues should be allowed, but changing <= to < means 255 upvalues are rejected while 254 pass. More critically, if the check is disabled (in builds without assertions), n=MAXUPVAL passes but the allocated closure only holds MAXUPVAL-1 upvalues, causing an OOB write in the loop.

Flipping <= to < in api_incr_top means the overflow check fires one slot too early in non-APICHECK builds (lua_assert path), but in APICHECK builds the assert fires before the slot is used. More critically, this allows L->top.p to reach exactly ci->top.p+1 when lua_assert is a no-op, writing one slot past the reserved stack space.

explanation: Flipping < to <= in api_checknelems allows n equal to the number of available slots to pass the check. Since the stack pointer arithmetic includes the function slot itself, this permits reading one element below the valid stack bottom, causing an out-of-bounds stack read.

Flipping < to <= in adjustresults means ci->top.p gets bumped even when already equal to L->top.p (the common case). This causes ci->top.p to be set to top.p when they are equal, which is a no-op normally but combined with other stack operations can push ci->top.p one slot past the actual top, corrupting stack frame accounting and leading to OOB writes in subsequent pushes.

Off-by-one: changing >= to > in the overflow check for newbuffsize allows sz == MAX_SIZE - B->n to pass, causing B->n + sz + 1 to wrap around, leading to a tiny allocation and subsequent heap overflow.
Off-by-one: changing >= to > means when exactly sz bytes remain, the code tries to use the full buffer anyway while writing sz bytes starting at B->b + B->n, writing one byte past the allocation.
Changing n <= 0 to n < 0 allows n=0 through, causing uv[-1] access (zero-indexed would be one before the array).
Flipping < to <= in the bounds check for CClosure upvalue access allows reading one element past the end of the upvalue array.
Off-by-one in positive index validation: < instead of <= makes valid top-of-stack index appear valid but reads nilvalue sentinel incorrectly.
Flipping < to <= in Lua closure upvalue bounds check allows access one past the end of the upvalues array, causing heap-buffer-overflow when reading name or value.

Off-by-one in api_checkpop's tbclist boundary check: flipping < to <= allows popping one extra element past a to-be-closed variable boundary, enabling stack underflow when the tbclist pointer sits exactly at the computed boundary.

Since newsize is size_t (unsigned), newsize >= 0 is always true, so when resizing to 0 (freeing), if allocf returns NULL the code incorrectly raises a memory error instead of accepting the NULL return as a valid free result.

Flipping < to <= in luaL_addchar's bounds check allows writing one byte past the end of the buffer when n equals size, before luaL_prepbuffsize is called to grow the buffer.
Removing the -1 from the table size calculation is a minor off-by-one but not directly a memory safety issue. However it over-allocates.

Flipping i > n to i >= n in luaB_select means when i == n (a valid index pointing to last arg), it gets clamped to n, then return n - (int)i returns 0 results instead of 1. While this is logic corruption, combined with the argcheck below it could cause stack underreads in edge cases.
